title: Iran Tells Pakistan There Will Be No Talks With the U.S. Until Its Demands Are Met
excerpt: Iran told Pakistan's army chief in Tehran on Tuesday that there will be no talks with Washington until its conditions are met, even as President Trump says a deal to end the war is largely negotiated.
content:
Iran has told Pakistan there will be no talks with Washington until Tehran’s demands are met, hardening its stance despite mediation efforts by Islamabad, the key go-between in the eight-month-old war, according to Reuters.

President Masoud Pezeshkian discussed mediation efforts and regional developments with Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, in Tehran on Tuesday, according to the Iranian outlet Nournews, cited by Reuters. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf told Munir that Washington could not regain Tehran’s trust until it fulfills seven conditions Iran set last month for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to an Iranian readout of the meeting. The demands include ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports, as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts, Reuters reported.

Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, delivered the same message in a separate meeting, saying all enriched nuclear material would remain in Iran, according to Iranian media cited by Reuters. U.S. Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy U.S. demands, Reuters reported.

Pakistan brokered a ceasefire in April and hosted direct talks that produced an interim peace agreement in June, but that Islamabad Memorandum unraveled when fighting resumed weeks later, according to Reuters. President Donald Trump has said a deal to end the war is largely negotiated and that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen, while Iranian leaders have denied that direct talks with the U.S. are taking place, according to Al Jazeera.

The stakes for Texas run through the strait: it is one of the world’s most important oil chokepoints, and oil prices spiked above $100 a barrel after the war began, up from roughly $65 before it, according to Al Jazeera. For now, the diplomacy remains stuck between a deal Washington says is close and conditions Tehran says come first.
